speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of this resolution because I believe it is high time we should apply ourselves to a scientific study of the economic conditions under which we are living. Banking to-day is not conducted scientifically, but there are many features about the art of banking which could be scientifically understood. Banking has reached its present status entirely by an empirical process. The bankers themselves did not realize what they were stumbling upon when they undertook to take care of the money of the merchants. If we go back into the ages when tokens were exchanged we can realize how it became necessary that there should be some small medium of exchange having in itself an intrinsic value to take the place of the leather tokens then in use. This medium of exchange became of such a nature that it was necessary that it be cared for and stored, and it naturally gravitated into the strong rooms of the goldsmiths. Although all the earliest bankers were not necessarily goldsmiths, in England this was almost entirely the case. Childs and Company and the other private bankers which disappeared in the nineties when the joint stock banks were consolidating or amalgamating or fusing were originally goldsmiths. In taking charge of the money of the merchants and in issuing receipts for it, the early bankers soon discovered that the money did not go out in the same proportions as it came in, that the receipts which they gave remained current among the merchants of England and even on the continent for several months. This was the beginning of our present day system of bank notes and cheques. The goldsmiths, scenting an opportunity of making money, began to issue receipts against gold which did not exist. As the practice of banking became more select and respectable, it was discovered that for every hundred units of coin placed in their hands, they had to reserve a percentage as till money. In the nineties that percentage ranged around 23 to 26 per cent. During the intervening years it has gradually fallen until to-day 10-6 per cent represents the amount of till money which must be retained against every S100 of coinage held by the banker. This means then that the banker has in his hands approximately $90 which he is not likely to be called on immediately to repay; and realizing that, he scents the possibility of making money. But he must be careful, because this money is a trust committed to him by the business people of the country; and so, out of trial and error, out of experiment and understanding, he has determined upon a percentage which is

loaned at call, a percentage which is loaned on short discounts, a percentage which is loaned on long discounts, and a percentage which is actually loaned out on almost permanent investment.
In the article Commercial Banks and Credit, in a book entitled What Everybody Wants to Know about Money, by G. D. H. Cole, I find, taking the London clearing banks' averages of weekly figures, the following percentages of deposits: In 1925, cash and balances with the Bank of England were 11-8 per cent; 1933, a decrease to 10-6 per cent. Money at call and on short notice, in 1925, was 7 per cent, and in 1933 it had decreased to 5 per cent. In 1925 bills discounted represented 13-6 per cent; and in 1933 it had increased to 17-8 per cent. Investments in 1925 represented 17-2 per cent; and in 1933 it had increased to 27-3 per cent. Advances- peculiar to British banking-in 1925 were 51-5 per cent, and in 1933, 39-9 per cent.
It will be seen that in the course of time, with a better understanding of business and the continued and increasing use of the cheque, the disposition of the banker has tended and now is to invest definitely and not on short call, for he realizes that he has at his disposal approximately ninety per cent of the money deposited with him. The range of $90 in each $100 is spread over these various loans, and I would point out that by careful and judicious lending, in terms from 6hort to long, the banker is able to carry the load. But if any one of his loans fails to come through on due date he must immediately hedge his bet; he must immediately attempt to cover up by calling in loans from the other terms; and it so happens that when a catastrophe overtakes the country, bankers, here, there and everywhere, are placed in the position of calling in their loans-first call money, then three months' bills, then six months' obligations, and so on. Every person who has received money from the bank is compelled to scratch in the corners to repay his debt.
I make the definite assertion, therefore, that the banks are the first institutions in our economy to encourage a depression and for the very same reason they are the last institutions in our economy to ease it and to encourage a boom. That is only natural from their very position. They find themselves unable to exceed loans beyond the amount of their actual deposits. It has been said in this house that if they receive $100 they are in a position to loan $900. Theoretically that is true, but actually and practically it is impossible because the banker must be at all

Banking-Mr. Brunelle
times ready to return, the money to the depositor and he fears that he may be caught betraying his trust.
But what do we discover in this matter of loaning out money which belongs to the people of the country? The banker has developed towards that money the attitude of regarding it as his own property and he earns interest on it in the loan, and so encourages us to apotheosize interest and usury on loans. The banker is not justified in charging interest on loans. That may sound strange, Mr. Speaker, but I say that if we are going to use the money and the credit of the country to lend out for the purpose of helping industry in certain directions, it should be done on the basis of insurance cost to make sure that that money shall be returned, and not on the basis of interest on the money loaned. We must have that money back and it must pay insurance that it shall come back. That feature can be accomplished only by a government, and I charge this government to take into consideration the fact that in developing credit for the purpose of encouraging the industries of the country it can be done in precisely that way. We should then do away altogether with the idea of banks encouraging loans to their own friends.
It is not difficult, going over the history of banking, to see how frequently this has been done or how much the wealthy patrons of a bank can obtain at reasonable rates of interest, while business men with indisputable security are finding it hard to get proper loans at decent rates. Loans should be divided into classifications, insured according to the risks in any particular classification, and that can be done only by a government. Consequently, in the consideration of this resolution, I urge that the government realize the importance of undertaking the whole system of credit and finance scientifically, studying it from the economic standpoint and instituting such changes as would make it possible for the government to own and control the chartered banks as well as the Central bank.
It is high time that the government inserted itself into the whole financial system of the country; there is ample reason for this to be done. It has been refused up to the present, but it will not be long before the government realizes that this is its only hope of salvation. Every private company and every public company, when it is incorporated, should allot to the government some proportional equivalent of its paid up and authorized capital. If I have a large tract of land and intend to dispose of it in lots or in small acreage, I cannot do so unless I
first give to the government for roads and highways some portion of my property. If a man dies and leaves an estate, part of that estate is immediately claimed by the government. If a man buys foreign goods, those goods cannot come into the country until some duty on them is paid to the government. There is no part of our public or industrial life from which the government is not taking something as its 9hare. But in the matter of finance nothing has yet been attempted, and whenever it is talked about the cry is raised, "hands off finance." But we shall have to come to it.
For these reasons, and because I feel that only in this way can we bring to the people a sense of the real responsibility which we have as people, I am prepared to vote for this resolution.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
I have listened with great interest to the speech which has just been delivered by the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). In one of his previous addresses he said that environment had a great deal of influence on the opinions of the people; and probably because I sit on the same side of the house as he does, although I do not share his political views, and because I hold some ideas closely related to what he has just expressed, I find myself almost in accord with what he has just stated. I was a little surprised that my hon. friends the member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and 'the member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) did not agree with the resolution, because after all it says only that the government should "consider the advisability" of national ownership.
I have great faith in the present government. I am certain that they will be ready to consider the advisability of controlling our central bank as well as the other banks. I am not in principle in favour of public ownership, and I take the accomplishments of the Canadian National Railways as a sufficient warning. But I think we need credit, and it is essential that credit restrictions should be ended. By refusing or by granting a loan a bank has almost daily the great responsibility of either keeping a man or an industry functioning or bringing bankruptcy to the door of that man or that industry. I realize that currency and credit are very important and complicated matters, but I think we all know enough to realize that easier and better credit would do a great deal to help our financial recovery. Our bank reserves are increasing; bank deposits are increasing, and I must say that at the same rate bankers' free advice to the public
Banking-Mr. Pelletier

is increasing. Good enterprises have been forced out of business for lack of credit. If bank loans were more freely given out they would help in all spheres of our life towards the financial recovery of Canada, because the amount of credit has been at all times and in every country a controlling and dominating factor. Since the banks have the privilege of creating money through the facilities that the government -has given them they should do more to help to accelerate our business and our trade. Bankers should not have so much say in the framing of our monetary law. After all the business of banking is not such a wonder, not really such a mystery; as I have heard it said, it is only a bookkeeping system whereby the privileges of the government and the deposits of the people are at the service of the bankers.
I do not believe in the slogan "share the wealth." I think it would kill initiative. Initiative is the creator of hope, of ambition and of happiness. But when we come to deal with a question as important as that of credit we ought to know who is to be the master in our country. Many of our great leaders have stated that the bankers should not have so much to say in the preparation of our monetary or fiscal laws and measures. It is the government of the country that should dictate those laws and measures in the interest of the people.
I intend to say no more than that I am in favour of the present motion, because it only asks the government to study the question whether our banks, the central bank and the chartered banks, should be owned and controlled by the government. While the government is studying these laws something should be done to lower the banks' rate of interest from seven per cent to five or possibly four per cent. I believe the banks in the meantime should discharge their enormous responsibility in a worthy manner; that they should do their share to promote our commercial recovery, and that they should set an example of true and practical patriotism by giving a freer line of credit to our traders and to the directors or heads of our commercial institutions.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
In speeches on this motion to-day there have been statements made which certainly need correction. In particular the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) stated that he was not one of those who believed that credit flowed simply from the point of a fountain pen. In order that there may not be any belief that certain people in the house have any idea of supporting such a view I

should like to place on the records of Hansard the social credit definition of what real credit is. I have as my authority The ABC of Social Credit. This is what it says with reference to that particular subject:
Real Wealth-Real Credit-Financial Credit
And yet with the facts staring us in the face, the preconceived idea that money is something tangible still persists. Some of us, like the most uncivilized savages, have made of it the fetish before which we pay our vain oblations. Money is not God, nor is it even a commodity. You cannot eat it, wear it, or live in it. Yet it remains a mental fixation with some of us that money itself is wealth. Money is not wealth. It can be considered as wealth only in so far as it can be exchanged for such goods or objects as we may desire. (A bag of gold' in the desert would little avail us.) The real wealth of any nation is its ability to -produce and deliver goods (including services) as, when, and where required. Similarly the real credit of a nation is the belief in that ability, whereas the financial credit of a nation is quite simply the estimate of that ability expressed in monetary form, or as it is called, "monetized."
That is how we define credit, so I would not want it to be said that certain people hold the view that credit merely flows from the point of a fountain pen. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) say that the people of Canada who supported the Liberal party in connection with that particular plank of their platform certainly expected that party to deal with the central bank just as has been suggested in this resolution; I know the people at large had that in mind. I should like to add that if the resolution also contained these words, "With the object of controlling the credit and currency policy of Canada" instead of referring to private banks, it would become a different proposition and would be exactly in line with the remarks made by the hon. member for Rosthem. If it is the intention of the government to introduce at a later date legislation which will have that end in view, I am quite prepared not to support the motion and to wait until the government carry out the promises they made to the people of Canada during the last election campaign.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are continually reminded that we should talk less and say more; if we did so we would not have so many empty seats in this chamber.
I am not prepared absolutely to support this motion because it suggests that the government should take over the control of all money. If that should be done we would not keep very much money in our pockets or in our houses, and I am not prepared to go as far as that. I like to have just a little bit of money that I can call my own. If the

Banking-Mr. Leader
mover would cut the tail off this resolution I would support it because, as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) has said, we campaigned on the issue of a national bank, nationally owned and controlled, and as far as I am concerned I am prepared to put into effect the platform on which we went to the country.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say
just a word or two in connection with this resolution. The hon. member (Mr. Coldwell) who moved it would give the impression that the group to which I belong are not in favour of public ownership; much stress was laid on that point. I should like to remind the house that our leader in Alberta said that if they could not get the cooperation of the banks they would establish their own state credit house, so there should be no misunderstanding in that regard.
I was wondering why we should spend our time discussing a resolution of this nature when the government are pledged to bring down legislation in regard to banking. It seems to me that it would be far better to dispose of this resolution as quickly as possible-indeed, it never should have come up -and then wait for the government to bring down the bill which we can discuss on its merits.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) say that fifty per cent of those who supported the Liberal party at the last election had done so because of the statement that the Liberal government would take over and control the Bank of Canada. I believe that if the people of this country had possessed confidence and faith in the Liberal party there would not have been any social crediters here now, or socialists either for that matter. If the Liberals had kept pace with the progressive changes that have taken place in every walk of life there would have been no third and fourth parties sitting in the house. We are here because of the protests of our constituents in regard to these matters.
It is evident that Canada cannot carry on indefinitely as it has been carrying on for the past number of years. The other day in the house a question was asked and answered as to how much interest this country has paid on its debt since confederation. The debt was given as $2,895,124,262.99; the interest paid amounts to 52,823245,404.93, so that our present debt just about equals the amount of interest that has been paid. If any hon. member cares to look up the Canada Year Book he will find that in almost every year since
confederation, when the debt stood at $75,722,624, there has been an increase in out national debt. I wonder how many of us who run businesses could carry on a business on that basis. We would soon be looking for the leakage; we would have to change our method of doing business if we went into debt more and more, year after year. So the time has come, in fact it is overdue, when this country will have to make drastic changes in its financial system, and I for one am anxiously waiting for the government to bring down the bill in connection with the control and ownership of the national bank. I think that is what we should be discussing to-day.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have come to the conclusion that it would be well for me, as the representative of a portion of this dominion, to place myself on record as to how I stand in regard to a publicly owned and controlled bank. I can do this with the greatest of ease because I was elected to support the present government, which stands for a publicly owned and controlled bank. I do not think we need to discuss that; we may leave it safely in the hands of the present government. Faced with a resolution worded as the one before us we are placed in a rather awkward position. Why did not the hon. member who introduced the resolution limit it to our national bank? Why did he bring in the private banks? I hold no brief for the private banks; I have done business with them for many years and have always found them good people with whom to do business. I have always paid them what I owed, and for that reason I had no difficulty with them. But with respect to a Canadian bank, a national bank for Canada, I would recommend that the government or anybody interested in the institution invite private interests and private bankers of Canada to keep their fingers out of this particular pie. Let us have a real nationally owned and nationally controlled bank. That is what I believe the Liberal party stands for. Therefore I cannot support the resolution in its present form, but I stand four-square for a nationally controlled and nationally owned Canadian bank.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much' of the time of the house in a discussion of a resolution which, I imagine, hon. members would not expect me to view with favour. I need not discuss at length the first part of the resolution, because the speech from the throne gave ample indication of the fact that the government is and has been considering the question of ownership
Banking-Mr. Dunning

and control of the Bank of Canada. From the interest displayed by hon. members in all sections of the house in all monetary and financial matters it is quite apparent to me that no government could avoid considering the matter, even if that were its desire; and this government does not wish to avoid considering it. I am sitting at the feet of many Gamaliels with respect to matters of finance, currency and economics, and I shall give such consideration as I am capable of to the Hansard report which will contain the various ideas submitted for lifting this country out of its difficulties.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: But do not adopt them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
As yet I have not heard anything new. That is not a criticism of the ideas expressed, but is merely an illustration of the old saying that there is nothing new under the sun. Since means of exchange were first devised between man and man, situations have arisen which have developed the kind of suggestion we have heard to-day and on previous occasions this session. I hope the mover of the resolution (Mr. Coldwell) will not misunderstand me when I compliment him upon his manner of presentation. If I may be permitted to say so, it was a happy change from the type of argument we have heard from that corner of the house to the effect that those who agree with the speaker and with the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are friends of humanity, and that all others are its enemies. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) got away from that type of argument, and addressed himself to the subject matter of his resolution.
I shall not attempt to go into all the intricacies of finance, but shall content myself by saying that I do not believe it would be in the interest of the people of Canada for the state to take over and operate the chartered banks of our country. I shall state briefly my reasons for that belief.
Apart from all considerations of a financial nature in the operation of financial institutions, I believe that the institutions of parliament and government have quite enough on their hands successfully to handle that which the constitution of Canada commits to their care, without trying to run all the business of the country from this chamber. Moreover, I do not believe that the machinery which has been developed through the years to enable people intelligently and properly to govern themselves in a representative assembly of this kind is the kind of machinery most effective for conducting the ordinary operation of any kind of business. One needs only to listen

in this chamber to the multitude of counsel with respect to any matter in order to understand how impossible and impractical it is for this to be an executive body. In fact, sir, we recognize that in our very institutions; we recognize it in the principles of cabinet government and the manner in which our British system relates that government to the legislative body, in the responsibilities which it places upon one and the checks it places upon the other. We see it in the provision demonstrated here every day whereby a proposal to expend public money or to tax the people must emanate from a minister of the crown, and be preceded by a message from His Excellency the Governor General. What is that but a check? It is a deliberately devised check, and one needs only to attend the sessions of legislatures in countries which do not have that kind of check, or one similar, to realize the very grave difficulties of attempting to charge a legislative body with any degree of executive responsibility.
" Oh," but you say-and I know the mover would say, and sincerely-"it would not be our intention to have parliament run the chartered banks; there would be a board." Yes, sir; that is the condition created as a result of the state going into business. Parliament creates a board to run this, and another board to run that, and so we have a series of bureaucracies operating the business of the country. I am not one who believes that private business is perfect. Like every other human instrument it is just as perfect as the individuals composing it; even parliament suffers from that limitation. Bureaucracy is subject to just the limitations of the individuals composing it. But, sir, it is subject to something more than that. A bureaucracy operating within a democracy, a series of boards operating the 'business of the country, have a tremendous self-perpetuating power. Think it over; they have a tremendous self-perpetuating power. One only needs to read the current history of countries which have developed this bureaucratic system which is advocated in the resolution now before the house in order to make a choice between maintaining to the utmost degree the kind of freedom which we enjoy in Canada, and bureaucratic control.

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: Has not parliament some control of the banks at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Of course, but this resolution intends that the government shall operate the banks or that they shall be operated through government instrumentality. Of course it is the function, indeed, it is the duty of this parliament, properly to control all

Banking-Mr. O'Neill
business and see to it that laws are put on the statute books and administered by the courts to ensure that business, and indeed our whole population, either as individuals or in their corporate capacity, shall keep in order and treat each other fairly. It is our business to make laws to ensure fair treatment as between man and man, as between institution and institution, as between individuals and institutions. But I submit, sir, that we should be losing something which is most precious in our national life if we so far sacrificed the kind of freedom to which I have just been referring in favour of setting up bureaucracies to run our chartered banks and our other business institutions. I do not know where we would stop if once we started that, and I am quite sure that the final result would be much worse than anything through which we have passed.
I do not wish to be misunderstood or misinterpreted as I am afraid my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was about to misinterpret me. I do not wish to be understood as indicating that any individual or any institution in this country should be free to do as he or it likes-far from it. It is our business to regulate by statute law the relationship between man and man, between industry and industry, and individual and industry, and that in all conscience, Mr. Speaker, is a big enough task. It is for that reason that I am against this resolution or any other similar resolution proposing to take over, without regard to anything else but the establishment of a socialistic state, the operation of business within Canada. We have gone far already in this country, and we may be compelled to go further, but for my part the going further will be slow.
As I said at the outset, I am opposed to the resolution in its present form, but in so far as it relates to the Bank of Canada the government is giving consideration to that question; and it will continue to do so.
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops):	Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak on this resolution, but before the question is put to the house I should like to make clear where I stand on monetary reform.
I am in accord with the resolution up to a certain point, and that is where it declares for the national ownership and control of the Bank of Canada, and if the resolution stopped there I would be prepared to vote in favour of it.
I am not prepared at the present time to quarrel with the mover of the resolution (Mr. Coldwell) as to whether or not it should be adopted in its entirety, nor am I in a position to quarrel with him to-day as to whether or not we should adopt a socialistic state in this country. But I do not believe it would be in the interests of this country to adopt a socialistic state at the present time, and if I had the power in my own hands to establish a socialistic state right now I would not do so.
I do submit, however, Mr. Speaker, that the issuance of currency and credit should be absolutely in the hands and in the control of parliament. I submit also that we shall never have, and never can have, any prosperity that is permanent in its nature so long as private individuals control the currency and credit of the country. You cannot have prosperity under those conditions. At the present time the taxation that is necessary to meet the interest on our bonded indebtedness and sinking fund takes almost fifty per cent of the money that we collect in taxation. How are you going to continue if you go on borrowing the money from private individuals owning and controlling the currency and credit of the country? How are you ever going to get out of debt? How are you ever going to do the things that are required by the people of this country as long as you have to pay tribute to private individuals to use something that belongs to the people? You can never have any permanent prosperity under that system.
As I said at the outset, I did not intend to speak on this resolution; I just wanted to make my position clear. Much time has been taken up discussing things that will all be the subject of discussion when the budget is brought down, and when the budget is brought down I am as firmly convinced as it is possible for any man to be that the Liberal party will bring down legislation that will bring about national ownership and control of the Bank of Canada. I firmly believe that, and I was elected because of the belief of the people of my constituency that the Liberal party had promised something of that kind. When the time comes, if the Liberal party are not prepared to bring in such legislation, then I am afraid I shall have to vote against the party, much as I should hate to do so. That is all I have to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, but when the question comes up of the national ownership and control of the Bank of Canada I shall have a good deal to say about monetary reform.

Banking-Mr. Coldwell

subtopic: PROPOSED NATIONAL OWNERSHIP AND CONTROL. OF BANK OF CANADA AND CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply very briefly to some of the points that have been raised.
First I want to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and hon. members opposite for the reception which this resolution has received to-day. Whatever disposition may be made of it, it has I think served a useful purpose in arousing a discussion and a frank statement by the Minister of Finance. I quite agree with him that an institution like parliament cannot be charged with the responsibility of running a bank or any industrial or business institution. It is unfitted to cope with such a task, but may I point out that no one suggests that. Those of us who hold the view that we have consciously to plan and integrate our economic life believe that subject to the statutes and powers laid down by the representatives of the people through the institution of parliament, those who are best able to plan and control the various financial and industrial institutions should be charged with that authority and that responsibility. The late government selected as governor of the Bank of Canada a man who is competent and skilled in the banking business, an able banking official. He understood the machinery he was to operate. I think it is along these lines that society will travel.
The cry against the number of bureaucracies running the country is generally raised whenever a measure of this description is proposed. Some years ago I looked up the speeches of Cobden, Bright and John Morley, who in their day and generation served Great Britain and society well. Again and again through those speeches I found that fear in connection with the proposed control of the bitter difficulties under which the people of Great Britain were suffering at the hands of the newly created industrialists. That particular cry does not frighten me at all. One of the criticisms levelled against the present situation is that we are governed by bureaucracies unseen and independent and, as the leader of our group sometimes terms them, irresponsible. They are irresponsible in the sense that they are not responsible to anyone but their own shareholders. I believe our financial bureaucracy is the greatest of them all and one which is perhaps responsible to a larger measure than any other for the conditions facing us to-day. The minister said that we might be compelled to carry out some of these proposals in the near future. I think we shall be, but I would like to believe that the people of this nation and of the world are becoming intelligent enough to be able

to anticipate compulsion so that compulsion will not be necessary. Compulsion is always disagreeable and sometimes changes brought about by compulsion act in a manner which many of us deplore.
So many hon. members have said that if the resolution stopped with suggesting public ownership and control of the central bank they would vote for the motion, but I may say that the reference to the chartered banks was designedly included in the resolution. Even if we have a government owned institution, even though our central bank may exercise, as such institutions undoubtedly do in certain other countries, a measure of control,
I believe the actual lending and other operations of the system will remain in the hands of the chartered banks. To the chartered banks will be left the actual decision as to what loans shall be made, as to what industrial enterprise is to be supported, as to what speculative business is to be carried on. I am not denouncing the bankers, but the fact remains that they are human and are looking out for their own welfare and profit and at times the preservation of the great interests with which they are themselves connected. I paid particular attention to the last hon member who spoke (Mr. O'Neill), who said that he believed there would be no prosperity as long as private individuals controlled our currency and credit. As long as the chartered banks remain in the hands of private individuals, so long will prosperity be deferred because, as I said a few moments ago, these bankers make the actual decisions regarding loans and credit.
Motion (Mr. Coldwell) negatived on division.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext:
Whereas, great numbers of Canadian seamen on the Pacific coast of British Columbia are out of employment and in many cases destitute;
And whereas, owners of ships and vessels of Canadian registry on the Pacific coast of British Columbia give employment in large measure to seamen, cooks and engineers of oriental origin;
And whereas, other countries give greater consideration to the employment of their own nationals on ships and vessels belonging to their own country;
And whereas, the Canadian government grant large sums of money to the owners of ships and vessels by way of subsidies;
And whereas, it is desirable that every encouragement be given for the employment of officers, seamen, cooks and engineers of white Canadian citizenship in preference to those of oriental origin on all Canadian owned and registered ships and vessels;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government take such steps as will provide for employment of greater numbers of white Canadian citizens on all ships
and vessels of Canadian ownership and registry, the owners of which receive sums of money from the public treasury of Canada.
He said: I did not expect this resolution to be called to-day, and so perhaps I am not as fully prepared to discuss it as I should otherwise be; but inasmuch as I have introduced it now for the third' time perhaps it will not be necessary for me to make as extended remarks as I have made on previous occasions.
The resolution is sufficiently self-explanatory, but before I get through I shall ask the courtesy of the house to allow a slight amendment, because the resolution as it stands does not go as far as it should. The resolution asks that the government shall take:
Such steps as will provide for employment of greater numbers of white Canadian citizens on all ships and vessels of Canadian ownership and registry, the owners of which receive sums-of money from the public treasury of Canada.
I am going to ask that the words "of Canadian ownership and registry" be deleted. That would mean that all steamship companies receiving subsidies from the Canadian treasury would be required to employ greater numbers of white Canadian seamen. I am going to-propose this amendment because, looking into-the matter more closely, I find that operating: in this country are large steamship companies whose vessels are registered in London, so that if I did not delete the words "of Canadian ownership and registry" the result would be that only those shipping companies whose vessels were registered in Canada would come within the terms of the resolution.
The first recital of the resolution is:
Whereas great numbers of Canadian seamen on the Pacific coast of British Columbia are out of employment ...
I do not think any hon. member will dispute that.
And whereas owners of ships and vessels of Canadian registry on the Pacific coast of British Columbia give employment in large measure to seamen, cooks and engineers of oriental origin ...
I realize that there are perhaps hon. members who do not see eye to eye with me in regard to the employment of white Canadian seamen as against orientals. I am not asking that no orientals be employed, because I know that on ships operating between China and the Pacific coast it may be necessary that some orientals be employed to take care of oriental passengers. But here we find the country paying out, as it did in 1931, some 1900,000 by way of subsidy to a steamship company which employs at least 4S0 orientals on each steamer and with only the nucleus of a white crew in charge.
564	COMMONS
Pacific Coast Shipping-Mr. Reid
I submit that it is just about time we took more serious note of the situation. I think every hon. member will agree with me that it is only fair for us to begin to look after our own people first. Practically every other nation in the world' has some stipulation with Tespect to its own nationals. It will be found that on ships subsidized by the United States the companies are called upon to have 100 per cent American crews; and the governments rijf Norway, Japan, China, Australia and other .countries insist upon the employment of their * own nationals on their own ships. These ^countries pay greater attention to that point tfibn we do.
The steamship companies in Canada declare that they cannot get along without all these orientals, but I would point out that from 1921 to 1930 no such large subsidies were given to these companies as we gave from 1930 to 1935, and they operated just the same. I am not forgetting also that we have more than
2,000	white Canadian seamen idle on the Pacific coast, and it is galling and very ill-becoming for high officials in this land to say, as some of them have done, that our own seamen are not as good as those from other countries. I take particular exception to that statement. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) not long ago pointed out that, at one time in this history of Canada, Canadian ships sailed the seven seas, but to-day we have practically none. Most countries today are learning that it was unwise not to pay some attention to shipping and maritime icraft. If we are to be guided by those nations that are now taking cognizance of that fact, *where shall we find the men to man ships in the future if we are to give preference to people born in countries across the Pacific?
When I introduced this resolution on a former occasion the then Minister of Trade and Commerce argued that the men employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on these large ships were British subjects from Hongkong. Well, anyone who has taken a little time to look into the exact situation in Hongkong will hardly make that statement very seriously. For the information of the house I might perhaps indicate how these people are engaged.
There is on board these ships a No. 1 man, a Chinaman, who on his arrival at Hongkong picks up a crew. Hongkong is a large city and it has only a small white population. I understand that there is practically no barrier in the city between the oriental population and Europeans, and for the No. 1 man to hire men in that seaport and then have the argument advanced that because they are hired

in Hongkong they become British subjects is to carry the point altogether too far. As a matter of fact, when the vessel docks guards are put around it to see that these men do not leave the ship.
As the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has truly said, these men are engaged because their labour is cheap; but when the steamship company says that it cannot discontinue the hiring of orientals because otherwise the cost would be too great,
I dispute that statement. If they had 100 per cent white crews on these vessels I doubt whether they would engage 480 men plus officers, as we find on each of the two steamers plying between the Pacific coast and China.
The statement has been made that if orientals are not employed our trade with China might be impaired. But let us look at the situation in Australia. They do not allow orientals to unload a cargo there, and there is a barrier in the language test to keep out orientals; yet the trade returns as between Australia and Japan and China will show that Australia has done more trade in the past few years than we have. For the benefit of the members of the house I might point out that last year subsidies were paid as follows: British Canadian Steamships, on the China service, $118,000; on the Silver-Java-Pacific line to South Africa, $84,000. Those payments to the company were made to encourage the movement of lumber, and when I made the statement in the house that I believed money was being handed out without very much consideration the then Minister of Trade and Commerce took it upon himself to send my speech to almost every lumberman on the Pacific coast. They in turn chided me for making such remarks, but may I point out that although the Silver-Java line were receiving $84,000 yearly to encourage the lumber industry they were actually charging three dollars a thousand more for lumber than the rate at which it could have been taken by other ships, and, due to the question having been brought up in the house and the department going into the matter, that steamship company then lowered their rates three dollars a thousand.
Then take the Canadian Australasian line, $200,000. By the regulations of the department two-thirds of the crew must be British. On the China and Japan service we gave last year a grant of some $690,000, and it is remarkable that in the agreement entered into be-

___	Pacific Coast Shipping-Mr. Reid
tween that company and the trade and commerce department the clause relating to seamen, officers and crew has been entirely left out, or, shall I say, rubbed out. In most of the others, if not all, there is some clause with regard to the hiring of officers and engineers. For instance, in connection with the subsidy to the British Canadian Steamships there is a clause relating to officers and engineers. A majority of all officers and engineers of the Silver-Java line have to be British. As regards the Canadian Pacific line between China and Japan there is no such clause at all. The steamers Niagara, Makura and Marama, of the Canadian Australasian line, which receives $200,000, must carry a crew two-thirds British. Of other lines receiving subsidies, some have clauses with regard to the hiring of seamen and others have not.
I think this resolution should commend itself to every hon. member and to the country. In plain language it is just about time we began to look after our own people. The reason the word "white" is inserted is, as I explained at the outset of my speech, that when men are hired from Hongkong the statement is made that they are British subjects. Some nationals on other steamship lines belonging to other countries are called upon to produce their birth certificates. It would be interesting if some clause were put into our agreements requiring that Chinese who are engaged at Hongkong shall produce their birth certificates, that is if they have one at all.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman whether these people from Hongkong would be Canadian citizens? They would be British subjects, but not Canadian citizens.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext: No. I have had that question put to me many times. The argument has been used in the house about Chinese from Hongkong being British subjects. I have seriously disputed that statement. As I pointed out, Hongkong is a large city, predominantly Chinese, with a European quarter, but how could any man say that a Chinese, simply by being hired in the European quarter, became a British subject? I believe that is pretty far-fetched, and I have disputed seriously and will continue to dispute the statement that the orientals in these ships are British subjects.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext: In any case they would not be Canadian citizens.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext:
They would not be Canadian citizens. In my resolution I am asking that every preference be given to Canadian; citizens. I hope hon. members this year can lend support to the motion. I know very often there is talk of brotherhood and of not raising racial barriers; yet I think it is inherent in us that we first of all have a little charity towards our own people. They should come first, in my opinion, especially during these troublesome times when over two thousand of our own Canadian fellow citizens are walking the streets in the cities of New Westminster and Vancouver.
I do not want to labour the matter at length nor to wander in great detail into figures. This matter came before the house last year and was referred to a committee. During the time the matter was being discussed in the committee, legal representatives of the Canadian Pacific railway, I think, and other steamship companies appeared before that committee and wanted to make representations on behalf of their companies. This I objected to at that time unless representatives from the seamen's union were also allowed to come before the-committee so that it might hear the two-sides and in fuller detail. Immediately that suggestion was made the representatives of the companies withdrew their request. If the house has any doubts on this matter, or if the minister is not prepared to accept the resolution as it stands on the order paper,
I should like to see the matter again gone into before that committee, and every opportunity given to the steamship companies to lay their views before it, with the proviso, however, that the seamen be brought before the committee so that they can combat or refute statements made by the shipping companies and so that every piece of information regarding the matter shall be placed before the members.
I have not taken time to go into the total numbers engaged in all those ships, but it runs into many thousands. As I have pointed out, it is just about time that we became sea-minded. We are becoming air-minded. We have two great coasts, the Atlantic and the-Pacific, and yet we are forgetting entirely the encouragement of those men whose calling is to go down to the sea in ships. There is an inscription above the door of this building:
The wholesome sea is at her gates
Her gates both east and west
566	COMMONS
Pacific Coast Shipping-Mr. Maclnnis
It cannot be very wholesome so long as we allow companies subsidized by this country to hire hundreds of orientals in Hongkong who in large measure displace our own good Canadian seamen.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext: Not knowing this matter was coming up, I am not so well prepared, so perhaps I shall not be so brief. I will support this resolution if representatives of the seamen's union will have an opportunity of bringing other abuses before the committee. While we at the head of the lakes have not so much water, we have a number of difficulties, three of which 'I should like to have considered: First, when a young man is employed on a boat .quite often he does not get a round trip. He is a long way from home and he has Ao ride the rails back. I could speak at -length on that point, but it is not necessary. Second, the wages paid on our Canadian boats are not in keeping with the needs of -our men nor with the wages paid by other companies. Third, when our seamen have to pass examinations for promotion, we suggest that at the head of the lakes examinations be held or transportation be paid for those seeking promotion.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OP ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in saying a few words on this resolution moved by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), I should like to commence by stating that I have two objections to it, though I do not wish to convey the idea that I am opposed to the sense of the resolution itself.
My first objection is that it goes too far; my second objection, which may sound rather paradoxical, is that it does not go far enough. I think it goes too far when it designates by colour the kind of Canadian citizens who are to be employed, and it does not go far enough when it does not suggest the condition under which these Canadian citizens are to work on ships in receipt of assistance from the government of Canada. I remember that when I was much younger than I am to-day I spent a few years in the United States, where I noticed that the negro was not in the same position, as far as citizenship was concerned, as were the white residents of that country. I took great pride to myself, being a Canadian and of course living within the British empire, because in Canada all citizens were treated the same regardless of race or colour. I hope
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
I was not wrong. I should like to believe
that I was right; that colour was not to be considered a factor in Canadian citizenship.
I suggest that it is not enough to state that Canadian citizens should be employed in greater numbers; I support the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) in that view, but we should remember, when we stipulate that these employees shall be white, we exclude not only people from the orient but also the descendants of people who came to Canada to escape from slavery, who thought they would be secure here, who expected to be on a level with the rest of the community. We are excluding these as well when we use the term "white" in this resolution. We also exclude the Indians, who certainly are Canadians if anyone in this country is a Canadian.
Then in my opinion the resolution does not go far enough when it does not provide that before the government of Canada gives any assistance by way of subsidy or otherwise, it should be satisfied that wages and working conditions on the ships subsidized are satisfactory for white men. Believing this would strengthen the resolution, I am going to move an amendment which I hope my hon. friend will see his way clear to accept. The amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Winn.peg North (Mr. Heaps), reads:
That the motion be amended by striking out the word "white" in the third last line of the motion, and by adding the following words to the motion:
And be it further resolved that all subsidies or monetary assistance by the government of Canada be withheld until such time as the government is satisfied that trade union rates of wages and working conditions prevail for all ranks on such ships.
The substantial part of the motion would then read:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government taks such steps as will provide for the employment of greater numbers of Canadian citizens on all ships and vessels of Canadian ownership and registry, the owners of which receive sums of money from the public treasury of Canada;
And be it further resolved that all subsidies or monetary assistance by the government of Canada be withheld until such time as the government is satisfied' that trade union rates of wages and working conditions prevail for all ranks on such ships.
